questions.stem: The boxed factors in this figure indicate where warfarin exerts its effect on the clotting cascade. What is the biochemical basis for warfarin acting on exactly this set of factors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They share a calcium-binding site independent of vitamin K

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are all synthesized by vascular endothelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are the only factors of the intrinsic pathway

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are all serine proteases uniquely cleaved by thrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: They are vitamin K-dependent factors requiring gamma-carboxylation

explanation.summary: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X and the regulatory proteins C and S, which are exactly the elements highlighted.
explanation.whyCorrect: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, blocking gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X and the regulatory proteins C and S, which are exactly the elements highlighted.

questions.stem: This figure illustrates how heparin acts on the coagulation cascade, marking its effect at factors Xa and IIa. Through what mechanism does heparin inhibit these factors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks platelet GPIIb/IIIa aggregation

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It chelates the calcium required by the cascade

choices.label: D
choices.text: It directly binds and cleaves thrombin

choices.label: E
choices.text: It activates antithrombin, which then inhibits factors Xa and IIa

explanation.summary: Heparin works indirectly by activating endogenous antithrombin; the activated antithrombin then inhibits clotting factors Xa and IIa (thrombin) in the common pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heparin works indirectly by activating endogenous antithrombin; the activated antithrombin then inhibits clotting factors Xa and IIa (thrombin) in the common pathway.

questions.stem: This chemical schematic shows mechlorethamine reacting with guanine bases located on adjacent DNA strands. What class of DNA lesion is being formed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pyrimidine (thymine) dimer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Depurination (abasic) site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Single-strand nick

choices.label: D
choices.text: Base-pair mismatch

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interstrand cross-link

explanation.summary: Nitrogen mustards such as mechlorethamine are bifunctional and covalently bridge the N-7 of guanine on two opposing strands, producing an interstrand cross-link that blocks strand separation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nitrogen mustards such as mechlorethamine are bifunctional and covalently bridge the N-7 of guanine on two opposing strands, producing an interstrand cross-link that blocks strand separation.

questions.stem: This figure links specific chemotherapy agents to their characteristic organ toxicities. Cyclophosphamide is mapped to the bladder; which urinary metabolite is directly responsible for that toxicity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acrolein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acetaldehyde

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cisplatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phosphoramide mustard

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mesna

explanation.summary: Cyclophosphamide metabolism produces acrolein, which concentrates in the bladder and causes hemorrhagic cystitis; mesna binds and neutralizes acrolein to prevent this.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cyclophosphamide metabolism produces acrolein, which concentrates in the bladder and causes hemorrhagic cystitis; mesna binds and neutralizes acrolein to prevent this.

questions.stem: In this diagram of where chemotherapy drug classes act across the cell cycle, why are the antimetabolite agents positioned to act specifically during the highlighted synthesis phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They block mitotic spindle assembly, which occurs during the S phase

choices.label: B
choices.text: They crosslink DNA in a cell-cycle-independent manner concentrated in the S phase

choices.label: C
choices.text: They interfere with nucleotide/DNA synthesis, which only occurs during the S phase

choices.label: D
choices.text: They arrest cells at the G1/S checkpoint before DNA is copied

choices.label: E
choices.text: They inhibit topoisomerase-mediated transcription unique to the S phase

explanation.summary: Antimetabolites are decoys for metabolic intermediates of DNA synthesis, so they are effective only during the S (synthesis) phase when DNA is being replicated; agents like alkylators act independent of cell-cycle phase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antimetabolites are decoys for metabolic intermediates of DNA synthesis, so they are effective only during the S (synthesis) phase when DNA is being replicated; agents like alkylators act independent of cell-cycle phase.

questions.stem: This diagram compares two classes of targeted agents blocking signal transduction at the same receptor. Why do the agents depicted acting inside the cell tend to cause more off-target adverse effects than those acting outside the cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They selectively target a single cell-surface antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are large proteins that provoke severe immune reactions

choices.label: C
choices.text: They bind extracellular receptors irreversibly

choices.label: D
choices.text: They enter the cell and competitively block ATP binding with relatively low target specificity

choices.label: E
choices.text: They can only be administered by continuous IV infusion

explanation.summary: Monoclonal antibodies bind the extracellular ligand-binding domain, whereas tyrosine kinase inhibitors enter the cell and competitively inhibit ATP binding at the intracellular kinase domain. Because TKIs are small molecules with less specific targeting, they interact with kinases beyond the intended one, producing more off-target adverse effects.
explanation.whyCorrect: Monoclonal antibodies bind the extracellular ligand-binding domain, whereas tyrosine kinase inhibitors enter the cell and competitively inhibit ATP binding at the intracellular kinase domain. Because TKIs are small molecules with less specific targeting, they interact with kinases beyond the intended one, producing more off-target adverse effects.

questions.stem: In the mechanism shown on the right side of the schematic, the small-molecule agent produces its effect on the receptor by which action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cross-linking two extracellular ligand-binding domains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neutralizing the circulating ligand before it binds

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degrading the receptor mRNA in the cytoplasm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binding the intracellular kinase domain to block receptor autophosphorylation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Competitively occupying the extracellular ligand-binding site

explanation.summary: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib bind the intracellular kinase (ATP-binding) domain of the receptor, preventing autophosphorylation and thereby blocking the downstream signal-transduction cascades that drive proliferation. This differs from monoclonal antibodies, which act extracellularly.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors such as imatinib bind the intracellular kinase (ATP-binding) domain of the receptor, preventing autophosphorylation and thereby blocking the downstream signal-transduction cascades that drive proliferation. This differs from monoclonal antibodies, which act extracellularly.

questions.stem: The adverse reactions illustrated are caused by an antimalarial drug. By what mechanism does this drug kill the parasite?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibits parasite dihydrofolate reductase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport of the parasite

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondrial function

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits conversion of toxic heme to hemozoin and raises lysosomal pH in the digestive vacuole

explanation.summary: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine block detoxification of heme to hemozoin and increase digestive-vacuole pH, causing accumulation of toxic heme that damages the parasite. Their adverse effects include pruritus, cardiomyopathy, and hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency).
explanation.whyCorrect: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine block detoxification of heme to hemozoin and increase digestive-vacuole pH, causing accumulation of toxic heme that damages the parasite. Their adverse effects include pruritus, cardiomyopathy, and hemolysis (especially in G6PD deficiency).

questions.stem: The adverse reactions shown belong to a first-line combination prophylaxis. What is the combined mechanism of its two components?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interferes with parasite 80S protein synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport and blocks folate (dihydrofolate reductase) synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification within the digestive vacuole

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

explanation.summary: Atovaquone selectively inhibits parasite mitochondrial electron transport, while proguanil's metabolite inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate/DNA synthesis. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and transaminitis (increased AST/ALT).
explanation.whyCorrect: Atovaquone selectively inhibits parasite mitochondrial electron transport, while proguanil's metabolite inhibits dihydrofolate reductase, blocking folate/DNA synthesis. Common adverse effects include nausea, abdominal pain, and transaminitis (increased AST/ALT).

questions.stem: The adverse effects depicted are associated with a tetracycline-class antimalarial. What is its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibits parasite protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binds parasite DNA and disrupts mitochondria

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification in the digestive vacuole

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cleaves an endoperoxide bridge to generate free radicals

explanation.summary: Doxycycline is a 30S protein-synthesis inhibitor that prevents the parasite from replicating. Its adverse effects include GI disturbances (diarrhea, vomiting, nausea) and photosensitivity, plus chelation with cations.
explanation.whyCorrect: Doxycycline is a 30S protein-synthesis inhibitor that prevents the parasite from replicating. Its adverse effects include GI disturbances (diarrhea, vomiting, nausea) and photosensitivity, plus chelation with cations.

questions.stem: The adverse effects shown are caused by an antimalarial used to prevent relapse of P. ovale and P. vivax. What is its mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inhibits heme detoxification in the digestive vacuole

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interferes with 80S protein synthesis and heme digestion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disrupts parasite mitochondrial function and binds parasite DNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibits mitochondrial electron transport and folate synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibits protein synthesis at the 30S ribosomal subunit

explanation.summary: Primaquine disrupts mitochondria and binds parasite DNA, and is uniquely active against exoerythrocytic (hypnozoite) stages. Its adverse effects include cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation), leukopenia, and hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primaquine disrupts mitochondria and binds parasite DNA, and is uniquely active against exoerythrocytic (hypnozoite) stages. Its adverse effects include cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation), leukopenia, and hemolytic anemia in G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: This schematic maps where FDA-approved monoclonal antibody therapies bind on the Ebola virus surface glycoprotein. By what mechanism do these antibodies neutralize the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blocking glycoprotein binding to host cell receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Blocking viral budding from the membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degrading the viral envelope lipid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preventing nucleocapsid assembly

choices.label: E
choices.text: Inhibiting the viral RNA polymerase

explanation.summary: The monoclonal antibodies bind the viral surface glycoprotein and block its engagement of cognate host receptors, neutralizing the virus; they also mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The monoclonal antibodies bind the viral surface glycoprotein and block its engagement of cognate host receptors, neutralizing the virus; they also mediate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.
